newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Saudi oil talks in Washington leave Riyadh smiling.
newsitem.headline: Saudi oil talks in Washington leave Riyadh smiling.

text.p: Saudi Arabia ended oil talks with the United States last week hugely satisfied with Washington's recognition of Riyadh as a reliable source of crude supplies, Gulf sources said on Tuesday.
Saudi Oil Minister Ali Naimi was in Washington last week as part of a large Saudi Arabian delegation led by Prince Sultan, the second deputy prime minister and minister of defence.
Gulf sources said the Saudi visitors left extremely pleased with Washington's formal recognition of Riyadh as a "secure, dependable and reliable oil exporter."

"I think this was the most important statement during the whole visit," said a Gulf source of the phrase which was used during Naimi's talks. It was publicly used following talks at the end of the visit between U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Prince Sultan.
The kingdom is the world's largest oil producer and exporter and the second biggest supplier to the energy-hungry United States, behind Venezuela.
The two sides agreed at the oil talks on closer and more regular contacts to review developments and their economic impact and positions on global warming.

Washington "agreed to share with Saudi Arabia its global warming research and data from its carbon dioxide sequestering programme. There was also an understanding for Saudi Arabia's position on this issue as an oil exporter," a Gulf source said.
"There was also agreement for more regular meetings and a mechanism for meetings if the need suddenly arises," he added.
Discussions on the possibility of leasing space in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) had not arisen because Riyadh preferred to lease commercial storage, the Gulf sources said.
"Saudi has its own storage and if the need arises for added space it would prefer to lease commercial space," on Gulf source said.
The Clinton administration wants to lease out unused SPR space in an effort to raise some $200 million in three years from 1999.
Details of purchasing the fighters, possibly U.S. Block 60 F-16s made by Lockheed Martin Corp were kept off the agenda during Prince Sultan's various meetings.
"They know what plane the Saudis want, the Saudis know what plane meets their requirement and the issue was not raised," said a source of the deal which has been under review for several years.

The purpose of the visit was to review the overall relationship between the two long-time allies and get acquainted with new officials in President Clinton's second-term administration, a Saudi source said.

"The two sides discussed Iran, Iraq, terrorism, the (Middle East) peace process and exchanged views of a wide range of issues. The visit was not focused on or aimed at reaching agreement on a specific issue," another Gulf source said.
